The Battle of Antietam was fought on 17 September 1862 along Antietam Creek near Sharpsburg, Maryland, United States. The Union army of General George McClellan stopped the first invasion of the North by the Confederate army of Robert E. Lee. With about 23,000 men killed, wounded or missing, it was the bloodiest single day in American history.

After a run of victories in Virginia in the American Civil War, Lee crossed into Maryland. He hoped to win support there, feed his army and persuade Britain and France to recognise the Confederacy. Union soldiers found a lost copy of his orders, but McClellan moved slowly. At Antietam he had about 75,000 men against about 40,000. He attacked in three separate stages: in a cornfield in the morning, along a sunken road at midday and over a stone bridge in the afternoon. That let Lee shift his men to meet each one. Lee retreated to Virginia the next night, and McClellan did not chase him.

It was victory enough for President Abraham Lincoln. Five days later he announced the Emancipation Proclamation, which made the end of slavery a war aim. After that, no European power would side with the South.
